title: What is the consulting career path, and what does up or out mean?
description: The levels from analyst to partner, typical time at each level, how titles differ at McKinsey, BCG and Bain, and what up-or-out really means.
hook: The consulting career path runs through about five levels, from entry-level analyst to partner, and "up or out" means you are expected to keep being promoted within a rough window or move on. Most levels last a few years, so reaching partner usually takes a decade or more. In practice, many people leave by choice well before the system asks them to.
body:
The levels, and what you own at each

Titles differ between firms, but the shape is the same: each level owns a bigger piece of the problem and more of the client relationship.

LevelMcKinseyBCGBain
Entry, from universityBusiness AnalystAssociateAssociate Consultant
Entry after an MBA or advanced degreeAssociateConsultantConsultant
Runs the project teamEngagement ManagerProject LeaderManager
Oversees several projectsAssociate PartnerPrincipalAssociate Partner
Owns clients and sells workPartnerPartner, then Managing Director and PartnerPartner

There are in-between titles too: Bain has Senior Associate Consultant and Senior Manager, McKinsey uses Senior Associate in some regions, and BCG has Associate Director in some offices. Big Four firms usually have more levels (often analyst, consultant, senior consultant, manager, senior manager, director, partner) and a longer route to the top. Our guide to MBB explains how the three firms differ beyond titles.

What the work looks like as you move up

Take one retail pricing project and follow it up the ladder:

  • Analyst: cleans the product-level sales data and builds the first charts. Success means reliable analysis: a clean model, a sharp interview summary, a chart whose headline the numbers support.
  • Consultant: owns a workstream, builds the profitability model and proposes which price tests to run. The shift is from completing a task to deciding which question the work should answer.
  • Manager: runs the team day to day, aligns the tests with the client's commercial team and turns separate analyses into one recommendation.
  • Principal or associate partner: shapes the project, steps in on hard client conversations and oversees several teams.
  • Partner: explains the decision and its risks to the executive team, owns the relationship and wins the next project.

Knowing this helps in interviews. When you are asked what you want to develop, you can name the step you are aiming for. What consultants do day to day goes deeper on the entry levels.

How long it takes

Most levels last roughly two to three years for people who progress steadily, and partners typically have ten to fifteen years of experience or more. Timelines vary by firm, office and individual, and strong performers sometimes move faster. Treat any precise number you read online with caution.

What up or out really means

At many top firms, you are expected to be promoted within a certain window. If you are not progressing, you will usually be counselled to leave, often with time and support to find your next role. It sounds harsh, but it follows from the shape of the firm.

Here is an illustrative example. Picture a team unit of 1 partner, 3 managers and 12 consultants. Suppose managers stay in the role about four years and consultants about three. Each year, about 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 manager seats open up, while 12 ÷ 3 = 4 consultants reach the point of promotion. If the firm is not growing, only 0.75 ÷ 4 ≈ 19% of them can become managers. If it grows 10% a year, it adds 0.3 manager seats, so (0.75 + 0.3) ÷ 4 ≈ 26% can move up.

The pyramid needs many more juniors than seniors, so not everyone can stay. That is why exits are built into the model, why alumni networks are strong, and why firms care about where their people land. Many people leave by choice for roles they want long before the window closes. Our guide to exit opportunities covers where they go.

How strictly the window is applied differs by firm and office, and specialist tracks often work differently. If it matters to you, ask about it in your interviews.

Entry points

  • From university: analyst-level roles, usually through an annual recruiting cycle and often via an internship.
  • From an MBA or advanced degree (PhD, law, medicine): consultant or associate roles.
  • Experienced hires: people with industry expertise can join at several levels, sometimes on specialist or expert tracks.

How consulting recruiting works explains each route step by step.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Up or out means most people are fired." Many leave by choice, and those who are counselled out usually get time and support.
  • "The same title means the same job." A BCG Associate is an entry-level role; a McKinsey Associate usually joins after an MBA. Compare by responsibility, not name.
  • "Promotion is about hours." It is about owning more of the problem: framing the question, managing people, earning client trust.

Practise now

1. In the team unit above, suppose consultants stay only two years instead of three, with no growth. What share can be promoted?

Show the answer

Now 12 ÷ 2 = 6 consultants reach the decision each year, competing for the same 0.75 seats. 0.75 ÷ 6 ≈ 12.5%. Faster turnover at the bottom means a smaller share moves up, unless the firm grows.

2. An interviewer asks, "Where do you see yourself in five years?" What is a strong answer?

Show the answer

Anchor it in the work, not the title: "I'd like to be running a workstream end to end and starting to manage a small team, ideally in healthcare, where I've already done some analysis. I want to get good at turning analysis into a decision a client acts on." Honest, specific, and it shows you understand the ladder. Avoid leading with an exit plan.

Where to practise next

If you are early in the process, start with what a consulting firm actually does, then begin case practice with our case interview guide.
